title: A Parasite That Gave Tens of Thousands of Americans Diarrhea: Can't Wash It Off, Can't Culture It, Can't Tell If It's Alive
dek: The oocysts behind tens of thousands of US diarrhea cases resist bleach and rinsing, and only become infectious after one to two weeks outside the body; labs can't culture them or test for viability, so outbreaks are hard to break.
why: This episode turns 'why outbreaks keep recurring' into a chain of evidence: it starts with tens of thousands of US cases, then shows the lab dead end of being unable to culture or test viability, and finally lands on what individuals can do about grocery shopping.
who: People working in food safety, fresh produce supply chains, or infectious disease control; also suitable for ordinary listeners who care about 'can I still eat imported salad' and want to understand US outbreak news.
skip: The opening chatter about syphilis can be skipped; the main thread starts around the 7-minute mark with the outbreak overview.

points.h: The US is in its largest outbreak yet
points.body: Daniel Griffin opens with the numbers: Michigan has surpassed 10,000 cases, North Carolina has another outbreak of about 1,000, and New York City has over 500. He calls it the largest Cyclospora outbreak he has seen, and shares his own kitchen clue—the pre-washed, chopped romaine lettuce his family ate came from the suspected Taylor Farms. The numbers aren't the point; the point is that these cases reflect contamination from two to three weeks earlier. By the time officials confirm an outbreak, the suspect lettuce is often already off shelves or eaten. This is the starting point for everything in the episode about 'why we can't get a handle on it.'

points.h: Cases appear two to three weeks after contamination
points.body: The mechanism is explained clearly around the 11-minute mark: oocysts shed in feces are not yet infectious; they must first sporulate in the environment for 7 to 14 days. After a person ingests infectious oocysts, it takes about another week to become ill. So a single contamination event takes two to three weeks to show up as the cases you see. By then, asking patients 'what did you eat a few days ago' misses the window; the leftover greens have been distributed and eaten, and the physical evidence is gone. This explains why tracing Cyclospora is so hard, and why cases are hard to link to a common meal—not because people forget, but because the two-week silent period makes the epidemiological question nearly unsolvable.

points.h: Rinsing and bleach can't touch it
points.body: Next comes a set of properties that surprise Vincent: oocysts resist chemical treatments like bleach and routine washing, and they are 'sticky,' adhering to leafy surfaces. So bagged 'pre-washed' salads aren't guaranteed safe; the problem isn't how long you rinse. A more fundamental lab obstacle is that it only infects humans, has no usable animal model, and cannot be cultured in vitro. That means Koch's postulates can't be fully fulfilled, and even testing whether a disinfection method works lacks an endpoint. PCR positivity only shows nucleic acid, not whether oocysts are alive or dead—something virology has long taught. The more you listen, the more you understand why the US sees outbreaks every year yet never finds the source.

points.h: It sporulates after leaving the gut, unlike Cryptosporidium
points.body: Christina adds the life history and corrects the intuition that 'oocysts must wait 7–14 days': the close relative Cryptosporidium is already sporulated when shed and can infect the next person immediately. Cyclospora, however, sheds immature oocysts that must sporulate in a warm, moist environment. The life cycle itself resembles Cryptosporidium: sporozoites invade small intestinal epithelial cells, multiply asexually as merozoites, and repeatedly infect new epithelial cells; later, some undergo gametogony, finally forming unsporulated oocysts that exit in feces. This 'wait outside the body' design gives it an opening to spread through produce supply chains—those two weeks in transport and storage carry contamination from the farm into countless homes.

points.h: An effective drug came before the pathogen was identified
points.body: The history segment tells a counterintuitive discovery order: treatment preceded pathogen confirmation. In the late 1980s, at the CIWEC travel clinic in Kathmandu, Nepal, many expatriates and trekkers had diarrhea lasting weeks. Technicians repeatedly saw small round bodies in smears but didn't know what they were. With no culture or animal model, researchers tried drugs based on coccidian diarrhea and found TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole/Bactrim) most effective. The pathogen was later described as a new species, named Cyclospora cayetanensis—the species name comes not from Nepal, where it was found, but honors the naming author's alma mater, Peru's Cayetano Heredia University.

points.h: US imported outbreaks could take root
points.body: The most alarming part of the latter half is whether the US could shift from 're-imported every year' to endemic transmission. Currently, most US patients have toilets and wash hands; oocysts go down the sewer, and the transmission chain breaks after the season, waiting for next summer's imports from endemic areas. But in reality, many low-income people live in multigenerational households, and farm laborers have restroom breaks controlled by employers, so they may relieve themselves in the fields. If that becomes common enough for oocysts to enter soil and irrigation water, and then get 7 to 14 days to sporulate, a domestic transmission cycle wouldn't need imports to sustain itself. Add that基层 (primary care) may not run expensive molecular stool tests, so hidden cases are undercounted—the host considers this a real risk.

points.h: Symptoms aren't just diarrhea; they drag on for two months
points.body: The clinical segment turns 'explosive diarrhea' into a concrete picture: watery stools five to fifteen times a day, large volume, and patients basically live next to the toilet. Daniel says the duration is the biggest surprise—not two or three days, but up to two months in immunocompetent people, and even months in immunocompromised patients. Don't treat it as just acute gastroenteritis: three to six weeks after infection, reactive arthritis can appear, and it can progress to Guillain-Barré syndrome. So when the US really sees tens of thousands of cases, the end-of-season public health burden isn't just diarrhea clinics; it includes delayed bills for neurological and joint complications weeks later.

points.h: Inactivation is only judged by looking for damage under a microscope
points.body: The finale is the paradox of testing and inactivation methods: the paper mentions UVC irradiation might help, but the verification method is still putting oocysts under a microscope to see if they look damaged—Daniel says that doesn't give him much confidence, because 'looking damaged' doesn't equal loss of infectivity. Molecular tests only look at nucleic acid and don't answer viability either; the current genome is even a draft with many gaps, about 44 Mb with high AT content—not that it can't be sequenced, but too few people work on it. The closer to the end, the more the guests admit: much of the knowledge is inferred from related parasites, and the original authors themselves repeatedly say 'speculate.' The real way forward might be to culture oocysts in vitro or in an animal model, or to use other Cyclospora species in the same genus.

terms.def: The episode's subject: a human-specific coccidian parasite that invades small intestinal cells via contaminated produce, causing watery diarrhea.
The resistant form of the parasite shed in feces; resistant to bleach and adheres to produce surfaces.
The process by which immature oocysts develop in the environment for 7–14 days to produce infectious sporozoites.
An autoimmune peripheral neuropathy that can follow infection; listed in the episode as a possible complication of Cyclospora infection.
Inflammatory arthritis appearing 3–6 weeks after intestinal symptoms resolve; a post-infectious complication.
